source.author: ov
source.text: Nunc quoque in Euboico scopulus brevis eminet alto gurgite et humanae servat vestigia formae; quem, quasi sensurum, nautae calcare verentur appellantque Lichan. At tu, Iovis inclita proles, arboribus caesis, quas ardua gesserat Oete, inque pyram structis, arcum pharetramque capacem regnaque visuras iterum Troiana sagittas ferre iubes Poeante satum.
source.text_original: Nunc quoque in Euboico scopulus brevis eminet alto / gurgite et humanae servat vestigia formae; / quem, quasi sensurum, nautae calcare verentur / appellantque Lichan. — At tu, Iovis inclita proles, / arboribus caesis, quas ardua gesserat Oete, / inque pyram structis, arcum pharetramque capacem / regnaque visuras iterum Troiana sagittas / ferre iubes Poeante satum.
source.text_english: Even now a short rock rises from the Euboean deep and preserves the footprints of a human form; the sailors, as if it could feel, fear to tread on it and call it Lichas. But you, famous offspring of Jove, when the trees that lofty Oeta had borne were cut down and piled into a pyre, order the son of Poeas to carry the bow and quiver and the arrows that would once again behold the Trojan realms.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: quin etiam Herculeo consurgit ab ordine Tydeus Nelidesque Periclymenus, quem parva Methone felevis Elis equis et fluctibus obvius Aulon caestibus adversos viderunt frangere vultus. Tu quoque Phrixeos remo, Poeantie, Colchos bis Lemnon visure petis, nunc cuspide patris inclitus, Herculeas olim moture sagittas.
reuse.text_original: quin etiam Herculeo consurgit ab ordine Tydeus / Nelidesque Periclymenus, quem parva Methone / †felevis Elis equis et fluctibus obvius Aulon / caestibus adversos viderunt frangere vultus. — / Tu quoque Phrixeos remo, Poeantie, Colchos / bis Lemnon visure petis, nunc cuspide patris / inclitus, Herculeas olim moture sagittas.
reuse.text_english: Indeed, too, Tydeus rises from the Heraclean line, and the son of Neleus, Periclymenus, whom small Methone, Elis famed for its horses, and Aulon, facing the waves, saw breaking the faces of their opponents with fists. You too, Poeantius, seek Phrixian Colchis by oar, about to see Lemnos twice, now renowned for your father’s spear, once destined to wield Heraclean arrows.
